bull_thesis:
The bull case starts with a measurement error and ends with a business that has quietly changed shape. Qualcomm's screened fair value of $59 and its margin of safety of -65% are produced by four valuation models all fed the same broken number: fiscal-2025 earnings per share of $5.01, down 44% year over year. Pulling the audited statements shows why that figure is meaningless. Pre-tax income rose from $7.44B (fiscal 2023) to $10.34B (fiscal 2024) to $12.66B (fiscal 2025) — compounding at roughly 30% a year — while operating income grew 22.7% in fiscal 2025 alone. What crushed reported earnings was a one-off tax charge that lifted the effective tax rate to 56.2% after two years at about 2%. The trailing-twelve-month earnings-per-share figure has already recovered to $9.32 as that charge rolls out of the window, and the latest quarter's earnings per share were up 173% year over year. Anyone screening this company on reported earnings is looking at an accounting event, not a business.

The second leg is what the market is paying for the corrected business. At $165.99, Qualcomm trades at about 13 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA), and roughly 14.8 times enterprise value to free cash flow, throwing off $12.50B of trailing free cash flow against a $175B market value — a 7.2% free-cash-flow yield, all of it returned to shareholders. Checked live on 27 July 2026, every named peer except one trades far higher: Texas Instruments at 28.7 times EBITDA, Marvell at 35.4, MediaTek at 42.2, Broadcom at 43.9. Only Skyworks, an eight-percent-net-margin radio-frequency supplier in structural decline, is cheaper. Qualcomm earns a 20-23% return on invested capital and a 55.4% gross margin on that base.

The third leg is that the pivot is real and is already showing up in reported numbers, not just slides. Automotive produced a record $1.33B quarter, up 38% year over year (reported 29 April 2026), passed a $5B annualised run-rate and is guided to exit fiscal 2026 above $6B — against an original fiscal-2029 target of $8B, since raised to $10B. Non-Apple chip revenue grew 18% in fiscal 2025, above management's own stated target. The fifth-generation automotive platform, shipping by the end of this fiscal year, is described as the largest generation-to-generation content increase in company history, with three times the processor throughput and twelve times the neural-engine performance, and the business is migrating from selling chips to selling modules with software attached — which raises both the revenue per car and the margin on it.

The fourth leg is the option nobody is paying for. At the 24 June 2026 Investor Day, management roughly doubled the fiscal-2029 non-handset revenue target from $22B to about $40B, with more than $15B assigned to data centre, and named Meta and Microsoft as customers. Adjusted earnings per share above $18 by fiscal 2029 was put on the record. First custom-silicon shipments to a large cloud operator are guided for the December 2026 quarter. At $166 the stock trades at roughly 9 times that fiscal-2029 target — which is another way of saying the market is assigning almost no value to the data-centre business at all.

The fifth leg is that management has earned the right to be believed on the near term. Guidance was beaten in all seven measured quarters, in each case landing at or above the high end of the range. More persuasively, the bad news was pre-announced: the memory shortage that is currently constraining the handset market was disclosed on the 4 February 2026 call, before it damaged any reported number, and the Apple chip runoff was volunteered with a figure ('a little over $2 billion' of fiscal-2027 revenue is 'a reasonable place to model the business', 29 April 2026). Companies that pre-announce their own headwinds with numbers attached generally are not hiding a third one.

Finally, the pricing lever has just been pulled. Bloomberg reported on 24 July 2026 that Qualcomm has told customers it will raise prices by a double-digit percentage to offset rising costs — the direct answer to the memory-inflation question analysts pressed on for three consecutive calls.

The conditions this case depends on: (1) the June 2026 quarter is in fact the trough in Chinese handset shipments, as management called it on 29 April 2026; (2) the price increases stick without triggering share loss to MediaTek; (3) the licensing annuity is renewed at roughly current scale; (4) the December-quarter custom-silicon shipment happens on schedule and is followed by a second named customer; and (5) automotive continues to convert its design pipeline at the current rate.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require the company to be bad. It requires the market to be right that this is a mature, customer-concentrated handset business wearing an artificial-intelligence costume, and that the costume is worth less than the 34% of market value the shares gave back in eight weeks.

Start with the base business. Handsets are roughly two-thirds of revenue and they are shrinking, for two independent reasons that compound. First, memory: chip makers are diverting capacity to high-bandwidth memory for artificial-intelligence data centres, and management stated plainly on 4 February 2026 that memory availability 'is going to define the overall scale of the handset industry' this fiscal year. Chinese customers responded by drawing down chip inventory, and Qualcomm has been shipping below true consumer demand ever since. Management called a bottom in the June quarter — that call is untested and lands on 29 July. Second, in-sourcing: Apple's chip revenue falls to roughly $2B by fiscal 2027 from a much larger base; Samsung sits at about 75% of its premium family rather than 100%; and on 30 June 2026 ByteDance — the very customer Qualcomm celebrated in February for launching the first agent-style artificial-intelligence phone on Snapdragon — was reported to be designing its own central processor for 2027 production. Every large customer Qualcomm wins is a future competitor once volume justifies the design cost. This is a permanent tax on the growth rate, and it never stops.

Second, the near-term numbers are going the wrong way and the market knows it. Consensus for the 29 July print is $2.22 of earnings per share on $9.68B of revenue, down roughly 20% and 7% respectively year over year. Fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings per share look set to land near $11 against fiscal 2025's roughly $12 — a down year. The screener's own forward figure is a consensus earnings growth rate of +1.2%. A business earning 15 times a declining number is not obviously cheap.

Third, the licensing annuity is the largest unquantified risk in the file and management will not discuss it. Licensing produced $5.58B of revenue at a 72% pre-tax margin in fiscal 2025 — roughly $4.0B of pre-tax profit, about a third of company profit, from an asset with no factories. Its largest single contributor is up for renegotiation with a counterparty that has spent five years reducing its dependence on Qualcomm. Asked directly on 4 February 2026, the answer was 'that's underway, and we don't have any update on that.' Asked again on 29 April 2026, the best available answer was 'we don't expect it to change' — a hope, not a disclosure. A one-third reset removes about $1.3B of pre-tax profit, more than the entire automotive segment earns today, at the stroke of a pen.

Fourth, the data-centre business that justifies the raised targets does not exist yet. Revenue today is zero. The fiscal-2029 figure of more than $15B was announced on 24 June 2026 with named engagements but no disclosed contract values, no backlog, and no committed volumes. Management's own first revenue milestone is a single custom-silicon customer in the December 2026 quarter. Meanwhile the spending is real and already dilutive: asked on 5 November 2025 why chip-segment margin fell despite revenue growth, the chief financial officer answered that 'data center is incremental to the investment profile that we have' — confirming the long-standing promise to hold operating expense flat has been deliberately broken. Research and development now runs at 21.4% of revenue. Qualcomm is entering a market where Nvidia, Broadcom, Marvell and the cloud operators' own silicon teams are years ahead, and it is doing so with a chip that has not shipped.

Fifth, the arithmetic of the headline does not close. Management framed total revenue 'toward $100 billion' by fiscal 2029 against roughly $44B today and a three-year revenue growth rate of +0.1% a year. Their own component targets — about $40B non-handset, roughly $30B handset chips, about $6B licensing — sum to about $76B. The gap between the components and the headline is promotional.

Sixth, nobody inside is buying. Zero open-market purchases against 62 sales totalling 37,387 shares. After a 34% drawdown, from a management team that has just told the market its long-term outlook doubled, the absence of a single insider purchase is the loudest silence in the file.

Seventh, the setup is hostile. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index entered a bear market in mid-July, down more than 20% from its June record; Bank of America described long semiconductors on 15 July 2026 as the most crowded trade ever recorded in its survey; and 'artificial-intelligence bubble' became the number-one tail risk in the same survey for the first time. Qualcomm's earnings land on 29 July, the same day as the Federal Reserve decision and two of the largest cloud operators' capital-expenditure guides. If those guides disappoint, Qualcomm's entire re-rating thesis — the edge-and-data-centre artificial-intelligence story — de-rates with the group regardless of what Qualcomm itself reports.

What would confirm the bear: a July 29 guide for the September quarter below roughly $10B; any indication that the price increases are being met with share loss rather than acceptance; a licensing renewal disclosed at reduced scale; or a slip in the December-quarter data-centre shipment.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market comes down to one arithmetic error and one framing error.

The arithmetic error is the earnings base. Qualcomm screens as a company whose earnings per share fell 44% last year and has compounded downward at 23.9% a year for three years, which produces a fair value of $59 and a margin of safety of -65% across four separate valuation models. All four are fed the same corrupted input. Fiscal-2025 pre-tax income was $12.66B, up 22.5% on the prior year, and operating income rose 22.7%; what destroyed reported earnings per share was a one-off tax charge that lifted the effective rate to 56.2% after two years at roughly 2%. The trailing figure is already back to $9.32 and the latest quarter was up 173% year over year. Four models agreeing with one another is not corroboration when they share a single broken input. Anyone running a mechanical value screen on this name is measuring an accounting event.

The framing error is what the sell side is actually underwriting. The street consensus target is $216.25, the median $220, with 27 targets in the last quarter averaging $207.26 — but the newest marks are drifting down, not up: UBS cut to $190 on 20 July with the stock at $172.60, having been at $235 on 25 June. Consensus forward earnings growth is +1.2%. So the street is modelling a flat business at a modest premium — it is not, in any meaningful sense, underwriting the data-centre programme. That is the specific assumption we think is wrong in both directions. It is too pessimistic on the parts that already exist: automotive grew 38% year over year to a record $1.33B quarter, is passing a $5B annualised rate against an original $8B fiscal-2029 target, and is migrating from chips to modules-with-software at higher margin — that is not a flat business. And it is too complacent about the part that does not exist: more than $15B of fiscal-2029 data-centre revenue with no disclosed backlog is not something to model at zero *or* at face value, and the street has largely chosen zero.

The second disagreement is on the memory shortage. The street reads it as a demand problem. Management's own framing, repeated across two calls, is that it is a supply constraint layered on top of a favourable mix shift — when handset makers must ration scarce memory, they allocate it to premium and high-tier phones, which is precisely where Qualcomm's content per device is highest. The chief financial officer said it directly on 29 April 2026: if volume shifts up, 'that is usually a benefit for us.' A shortage that shrinks units while enriching mix is a very different thing from a demand recession, and the 24 July 2026 report that Qualcomm is pushing through double-digit price increases is evidence the company holds the pricing end of that relationship.

The third disagreement runs the other way, and it is why we are not more aggressive. The street is not pricing the licensing renewal at all, and neither is management discussing it. Roughly $4.0B of pre-tax profit — about a third of company profit at a 72% margin — sits inside a negotiation whose terms, timing and counterparty posture are entirely unobservable from outside. 'We don't expect it to change' (29 April 2026) is the strongest statement on the record. That is the one place where the market's complacency and ours coincide, and it is the risk that would break this thesis without warning.
forcing_function:
Three dated events, in order of proximity.

1. **29 July 2026, after the close — third-quarter fiscal 2026 results and September-quarter guidance.** Confirmed by the company's scheduling notice of 15 July. This is the near-term forcing function and it resolves three questions at once: whether the June quarter was the bottom in Chinese handset shipments as management claimed on 29 April; whether the double-digit price increases reported by Bloomberg on 24 July are being accepted by customers; and whether the December-quarter custom-silicon shipment to a large cloud operator is on schedule. Note the caution: it lands the same day as the Federal Reserve decision and the Microsoft and Meta capital-expenditure guides, so a company-specific good result can be drowned by a sector-wide bad one.

2. **The December 2026 quarter — first data-centre revenue.** Management stated on 29 April 2026 that it is 'entering the custom silicon space beginning our ramp with a leading hyperscaler' with 'initial shipments in the December quarter'. This is the event that converts the fiscal-2029 target from a slide into an income-statement line. Until a dollar of data-centre revenue is reported, the market is entitled to value that business at zero, and it broadly does. The first reported figure — whatever its size — is the moment the discount becomes indefensible or the bear case is proved.

3. **Undated but binding when it lands — the licensing renewal.** The largest licence in a segment producing about $4.0B of pre-tax profit is in renegotiation, confirmed as 'underway' on 4 February 2026 with no update since. This is the only event in the file that can move a third of company profit in a single disclosure, and it will arrive without a scheduled date. It is as likely to force a re-rating upward — by removing the overhang at unchanged scale — as downward.

On the activist and sum-of-the-parts lens: there is no realistic activist path here. The parts discount is real but is not the sort a shareholder campaign can unlock — nobody is going to argue that a company earning a 20-23% return on invested capital, returning 100% of free cash flow and retiring 7% of its shares in two years is misallocating capital. There is no governance reset available and no strategic process to force. The re-rating, if it comes, has to be earned through the income statement.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is unusually short and unusually dense, and it starts in two days.

The immediate hazard is the 29 July results themselves. Consensus is $2.22 of earnings per share on $9.68B of revenue — down about 20% and 7% year over year — so the quarter is guided to be bad and the question is only the September guide. Management called the June quarter the bottom for Chinese handset shipments on 29 April 2026; if that call is wrong, or if the memory constraint has worsened, the September guide comes in below roughly $10B and the shares have no valuation floor to fall back on. There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall here — net debt is $5.47B against $12.50B of annual free cash flow, and the solvency score of 6.1 is comfortably safe — so the risk is entirely to the multiple, not to the balance sheet.

The compounding hazard is the calendar around it. The print lands inside the densest event cluster of the year: the Federal Reserve meets 28-29 July under a chair whose December rate rise is still the priced base case, Microsoft and Meta report on 29 July and Apple and Amazon on 30 July, and those four capital-expenditure guides are the market's verdict on artificial-intelligence spending. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is already in a bear market, more than 20% below its June record; Bank of America's July survey called long semiconductors the most crowded trade ever recorded and put 'artificial-intelligence bubble' as the number-one tail risk for the first time. A hyperscaler guide-down on 29 or 30 July de-rates Qualcomm regardless of what Qualcomm itself reports, because the entire re-rating case is an artificial-intelligence-at-the-edge-and-in-the-data-centre story. Catalysts resolving inside this cluster tend to produce muted or delayed re-ratings; early-August landings are cleaner.

The slower hazards over the next three to nine months are three. First, the memory shortage is not forecast to resolve: memory makers have guided to satisfying only 50-70% of demand with shortages running into 2028, and management explicitly declined to predict when it ends ('we can't really predict if this will continue for 2027 or 2028', 4 February 2026). Fiscal 2027 could be a second constrained year. Second, the double-digit price increases reported on 24 July are a bet — if MediaTek does not follow, Qualcomm trades margin for share in the one market (China) where the competition is a genuine two-player fight. Third, the data-centre spend is incremental operating expense that lands before any revenue: the chief financial officer confirmed on 5 November 2025 that 'data center is incremental to the investment profile that we have', and research spending is already 21.4% of revenue. Margins compress first and recover only if the December-quarter shipment leads somewhere.

The unbounded hazard, with no date attached, is the licensing renewal. It could be disclosed at any time, in either direction, and roughly a third of company profit sits on the outcome.
positioning_washout:
Forced selling is not the mechanism here — there is no dividend cut, no index deletion and no covenant to breach — but the ownership base is unstable in a subtler and more relevant way, and part of the wash-out has already happened.

Qualcomm has just been through the mechanical part. The shares closed at $250 on 3 June 2026 and $165.94 on 27 July, a 34% fall in eight weeks on heavy volume — 47.1M shares on 18 June, 37.1M on 26 June, 34.9M on 25 June, against a recent daily norm nearer 10M. That is what a crowded trade unwinding looks like, and the timing is the tell: the largest volume days cluster around the 24 June Investor Day, which was good news. A stock that falls 19% in the month after doubling its long-term targets, on rising volume, is being sold by holders who do not care what the targets say. Bank of America's July survey describing long semiconductors as the most crowded trade ever recorded names the seller: momentum and thematic money that arrived for the artificial-intelligence trade and is leaving because the sector broke, not because Qualcomm did.

The remaining fragility is the composition of who is left. Qualcomm sits in a genuinely awkward place in the ownership landscape. Its 2.2% dividend yield (a $0.92 quarterly payment declared 17 July 2026, payable 24 September) and 7.2% free-cash-flow yield make it a natural holding for income and quality-value funds — but those investors do not want a company spending 21.4% of revenue on research to enter the data-centre market against Nvidia. Meanwhile growth and artificial-intelligence funds will not own it at a 15-times multiple with two-thirds of revenue in handsets and a fiscal-2026 earnings decline. Each cohort has a reason to sell into the other's thesis. The recent thirteen-F filings visible in the tape are one-directional: Allspring cut 38.7%, Bank of Nova Scotia 20.3%, Bradley Foster 12.4%.

The insider record confirms nobody internal is stepping in: zero open-market purchases against 62 sales totalling 37,387 shares. The buyer of last resort is the company itself — Qualcomm returns 100% of free cash flow to shareholders and has retired about 7% of the share count in two years, which puts a persistent bid of roughly $2B a quarter underneath the stock. That is real support, but it is a slow bid, not a floor.

The practical implication: a disappointing 29 July guide would land on a shareholder base with no natural holder of the story, and the second leg down could be sharper than the first. Conversely, if the guide is merely adequate, the marginal seller has already left.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good business that has just been sold hard for reasons that have very little to do with it, priced at a real but ordinary discount, two days ahead of a print it has already warned will be weak. All three of those clauses matter, and they pull in different directions.

Start with what is genuinely mispriced. The screened case for Qualcomm — a fair value of $59, a margin of safety of -65%, earnings falling 44% — is an artefact. Fiscal-2025 pre-tax income was $12.66B, up 22.5%, and the reported earnings collapse was a single tax charge that pushed the effective rate to 56.2% after two years near 2%. Four of the five valuation models the screener runs are fed that broken number and therefore agree with one another for the same wrong reason. The corrected business earns a 20-23% return on invested capital and a 55.4% gross margin, generates $12.50B of free cash flow against a $175B market value, carries only $5.47B of net debt, and returns every dollar of that cash to shareholders. It trades at 13 times enterprise value to EBITDA while Texas Instruments trades at 28.7, Marvell at 35.4, MediaTek at 42.2 and Broadcom at 43.9. The peer file's premise that MediaTek is the cheap comparable is simply out of date.

Now the discipline. Part of that peer gap is earned, not stolen: those companies already report artificial-intelligence data-centre revenue and Qualcomm reports none. The fiscal-2029 target of more than $15B was announced a month ago with named customers but no backlog, and first shipments are a December-quarter event. Valuing that programme somewhere between the market's zero and management's face value is the whole of the analytical work, and doing it honestly produces a base-case sum-of-the-parts of about $202 — roughly 22% above today's $166, below the street's $216 consensus, and below the screener's own cash-flow fair value of $206. That is a real discount. It is not a fat one, and it is not the 65% the screen advertises.

Against that sits an adverse case at $130 that is about equally far away. Getting there requires the memory constraint to persist through fiscal 2027, the licensing annuity to reset lower, and the data-centre programme to be worth nothing — three things that could each happen and would compound if they did. The upside tail at $276 is fatter than the downside tail, so the distribution is right-skewed, but the base case is close to symmetric and there is no structural floor: Qualcomm carries net debt, not net cash, so nothing in the balance sheet stops the price.

On timing, the regime is the deciding vote. Earnings land 29 July, inside the densest event cluster of the year — the Federal Reserve on 28-29 July, Microsoft and Meta on 29 July, Apple and Amazon on 30 July — with the semiconductor index already in a bear market, the sector named as the most crowded trade ever recorded, and artificial-intelligence capital expenditure sitting as the market's number-one tail risk. Both legs of this thesis resolve on that single shared factor: the data-centre leg obviously, and the handset leg through memory pricing, which is itself a derivative of artificial-intelligence data-centre demand. A book that requires its positions to resolve on independent drivers cannot treat this as an independent one. Buying two days before a guided-down print, inside that cluster, is paying for optionality on someone else's earnings call.

So: wait for the wash-out, and name it. Two specific developments would change the call. The first is the 29 July guide itself — a September-quarter revenue guide at or above roughly $10.5B, together with confirmation that the price increases are holding and the December-quarter data-centre shipment is on schedule, removes the near-term uncertainty and makes the discount actionable at whatever price follows. The second is price: a guide-down that takes the shares toward $140-145 would put the stock at roughly 13 times a trough earnings figure with the data-centre business free, which is a materially better entry than today's.

Separately, and this is the more important number for a value book: judged purely on the price against the parts and on the quality of the numbers underneath, ignoring the calendar entirely, this scores well. The forensics are clean — seven guidance beats in seven quarters, headwinds pre-announced with figures attached rather than explained afterwards, a balance sheet with five months of free cash flow in net debt, and an apparent earnings collapse that dissolves on inspection. The moat is narrow rather than wide: a patent annuity that cannot grow faster than the handset market and gets renegotiated, plus a genuine engineering lead in a market shared with one strong competitor and populated by customers who periodically become competitors. It is stable rather than eroding — margins are holding, non-Apple chip revenue grew 18% last year, automotive is compounding at 38% — but the company is spending more (21.4% of revenue on research) to hold the same return, which is the definition of stable rather than widening. What withholds the top mark is not the business and not the numbers; it is that a 22% discount to a carefully-built parts value is a good price, not a great one. If this traded at $140 the answer would be different.

interrogator_dossier:
# QUALCOMM Incorporated (QCOM) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Listing analysed:** NASDAQ ordinary shares (QCOM), quoted in US dollars · **Reporting currency:** US dollars
**Live price used:** $165.99 (NASDAQ, 2026-07-27; previous close $166.97; 52-week range $121.99–$259.92; market value about $175B)
**Transcripts reviewed:** five consecutive quarterly earnings calls — 2025-04-30 (fiscal Q2 2025), 2025-07-30 (fiscal Q3 2025), 2025-11-05 (fiscal Q4 and full-year 2025), 2026-02-04 (fiscal Q1 2026), 2026-04-29 (fiscal Q2 2026)

A word on what has just happened to the price, because it frames everything below. Qualcomm closed at $250 on 3 June 2026 and trades at $166 today — a fall of about 34% in eight weeks. Nothing the company said caused it. In the middle of that decline, on 24 June, management held an Investor Day and roughly doubled its most important long-term target. The stock jumped 8% the next day, to $205, and then kept bleeding. The drawdown is a sector event — the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index entered a bear market in mid-July, down more than 20% from its June record — landing on a company whose own numbers are about to get worse for two quarters for reasons management flagged in advance. The committee's job is to separate those two things.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across these five calls the story does not wander; it widens, in three deliberate steps, and then runs into a supply shock the company does not control.

**Spring 2025 — diversification as defence.** The 2025-04-30 call is a company managing a known subtraction. Apple is designing Qualcomm's modem out of its phones, and the entire narrative is built to answer "what replaces it." The frame is a set of fiscal-2029 targets set at a 2024 investor day: $22B of combined automotive and internet-of-things revenue, $8B of that automotive, $4B from personal computers, $2B from extended reality (headsets and smart glasses). The chief executive's closing line is defensive in the most literal sense — "we always ask ourselves, is our technology relevant?" The chief financial officer explains that operating expense is being *moved*, not added: investment shifts out of handsets into the new areas while total spending holds flat. That is a disciplined, low-risk pivot, and it is what the company was selling in April 2025.

**Summer to autumn 2025 — the data centre arrives.** The 2025-07-30 call introduces an entirely new leg: Qualcomm is building artificial-intelligence inference accelerator cards and custom server processors, has agreed to buy Alphawave (a high-speed connectivity intellectual-property business) for $2.4B, and is "in advanced discussions with a leading hyperscaler" — one of the giant cloud operators. Revenue, management says, would begin in fiscal 2028. ## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

This is where the screener's own inputs need repairing before anything else can be judged.

**The headline earnings collapse is a tax artefact, not an operating one.** The screener shows fiscal-2025 earnings per share of $5.01, down 44.2% year over year, and a three-year compound decline of 23.9%. That looks like a business falling apart. It is not what happened. Pulling the audited income statements:

| Fiscal year | Revenue | Pre-tax income | Tax expense | Effective tax rate | Net income | Diluted EPS |

| 2023 | $35.82B | $7.44B | $0.10B | 1.4% | $7.23B | $6.42 |
| 2024 | $38.96B | $10.34B | $0.23B | 2.2% | $10.14B | $8.98 |

Operating income rose from $10.07B to $12.36B in fiscal 2025, up 22.7%. What destroyed reported earnings per share was a one-off tax charge that pushed the effective rate to 56% after two years at roughly 2%. The trailing-twelve-month figure has already recovered to $9.32 as that charge rolls out of the window, and the latest quarter's earnings per share was up 173% year over year — which is the same artefact running in reverse.

This matters because it contaminates four of the five valuation models the screener runs. The earnings-power, Graham and fifteen-percent-return models all show a margin of safety of -100%, and the Buffett model returns a fair value of $59 against a $166 price. Those models are being fed a tax-crushed earnings figure. The one model built on cash flow rather than reported earnings — the discounted cash-flow model, at $206 — is the only one whose input was not broken. When four models built on the same corrupted input agree with each other, that is not confirmation; it is one error counted four times.

**Growth claims versus delivery.**

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify.** The $100B revenue framing. Trailing revenue is about $44B. ## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Rising on strategy, falling on the near-term — and the two have decoupled.**

- **2025-04-30 — guarded.** "As we navigate those times, this is a company that is not — it's experienced a little of uncertainty. We always ask ourselves, is our technology relevant?" That is a chief executive answering a question nobody asked out loud. Language is defensive: navigate, uncertainty, relevant.
- **2025-07-30 — opening a door.** The data-centre section is hedged with care: "while we are in the early stages of this expansion," "if successful, we expect revenues to begin in the fiscal '28 time frame." Conditional verbs throughout.
- **2025-11-05 — assertive.** "We're probably one of the few companies among all the semiconductor companies that can go from 5 watts to 500 watts." Products have part numbers, a customer has a megawatt figure, and an investor event is promised. The conditionals are gone.
- **2026-02-04 — split.** Record revenue delivered with confidence; the memory constraint delivered without spin. On whether the shortage runs into 2027 or 2028: "We can't really predict." That is an honest non-answer, and it is worth more than a confident guess.
- **2026-04-29 — highest conviction of the five calls, on the long term only.** "We are in a period of profound change, and it may not yet seem obvious to the financial community" is a chief executive telling the market it is wrong. Simultaneously the handset commentary is the most cautious in the set: under-shipping demand, calling a bottom, sell-side models for the Apple chip business validated at "a little over $2 billion" for fiscal 2027.

The shift from offensive to defensive language happened in one place only — handsets — while the language around everything else moved decisively the other way. That is the signature of a real pivot rather than a cover story.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: High.**

Every quarter in the file was guided and then beaten:

| 2025-04-30 (fiscal Q2 2025) | $2.82 | $2.85 | Beat |

That reconciles exactly with the screener's seven-for-seven beat rate. The pattern is mild, consistent sandbagging: guidance ranges are set so that "high end" is the routine outcome. Revenue beats are smaller than earnings beats, which points to cost and mix discipline rather than demand surprises.

More telling than the beat rate is the *disclosure* record. Three specific forward statements can now be checked. First, the memory shortage: flagged 2026-02-04 as an industry-wide constraint that would define handset scale for the year — subsequently confirmed by the whole industry. Second, the Samsung share step-down to about 75%: stated in April 2025 and repeated unchanged in February 2026, exactly as forecast. Third, the Apple chip runoff: rather than obscure it, the chief financial officer volunteered on 2026-04-29 that sell-side models of "a little over $2 billion" for fiscal 2027 are "a reasonable place to model the business."

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The Apple licence renewal — deflected twice, and it is the single largest unquantified item.** On 2026-02-04, asked directly, the answer was: "whenever we see a renewal date on the horizon, we start discussions very well in advance. And so that's underway, and we don't have any update on that." On 2026-04-29 the chief financial officer went as far as "pending the renegotiation, the royalty, we don't expect it to change, right? It should be in the same scale that it's at." That is a hope, not a disclosure. The licensing segment produced $5.58B of revenue at a 72% pre-tax margin in fiscal 2025 — roughly $4.0B of pre-tax profit, about a third of the company's total — and its largest single contributor is up for renegotiation with a counterparty that has spent five years reducing its dependence on Qualcomm.

**Margin under memory inflation — asked repeatedly, answered obliquely.** Analysts pressed on this three times (2025-11-05, 2026-02-04, 2026-04-29). The answers all route to the same place: premium mix is a margin benefit, so a smaller but richer market is fine. That is true as far as it goes, and the price action outside the calls now supports it — Bloomberg reported on 24 July 2026 that Qualcomm has told customers it will raise prices by a double-digit percentage. But the calls never quantified the cost headwind.

**The data centre — the question analysts keep asking and cannot get sized.** Ben Reitzes of Melius pushed twice (2025-11-05, 2026-02-04) to get the opportunity framed against the old $2B extended-reality target. The chief executive's most concrete answer was "here's what I can say without front running our investor event." The Investor Day then gave the number ($15B+ by fiscal 2029) but not the mechanism: no disclosed contract values, no backlog, no committed volumes.

**What analysts are not pressing that they should be.** Customer in-sourcing beyond Apple. Samsung's internal silicon is discussed as settled at a 75% share. But in the same period covered by these calls, ByteDance — described on 2026-02-04 as launching the first agent-style artificial-intelligence phone on a Snapdragon chip — was separately reported (30 June 2026) to be designing its own central processor for 2027 production. Every large customer Qualcomm signs is also a potential future competitor for the same silicon. That structural tension is absent from the questions.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **The fiscal-2029 targets are large, recent, and unbacked by disclosed contracts.** The non-handset target moved from $22B to about $40B in a single announcement (2026-06-24), with more than $15B assigned to a business that has zero revenue and, as one commentator put it bluntly, chips that do not yet exist. Management's own guidance is that data-centre revenue begins in the December 2026 quarter with a single custom-silicon customer.

🔴 **Insiders are not buying.** Over the measured window there were zero open-market purchases against 62 sales totalling 37,387 shares. The screener's headline insider ratio of 0.00 understates this — on open-market activity alone, the direction is one-way. After a 34% drawdown, the absence of a single insider purchase is a real signal.

🔴 **The next two quarters are guided to be worse.** Consensus for the 29 July print is a roughly 20% year-over-year earnings decline, with the company under-shipping true demand while Chinese customers draw down inventory. Management called the June quarter the bottom; that call has not yet been tested.

🔴 **Customer concentration cuts both ways and keeps cutting.** Apple chip revenue falls to roughly $2B by fiscal 2027, Samsung sits at about 75% of its premium family, and the China business is a two-player market shared with MediaTek. Three of the largest customers each have a live path to less Qualcomm content.

🔴 **The personal-computer target has gone quiet.** A specific share number was published twice and then dropped. In an otherwise disclosure-generous file, silence stands out.

🟢 **The apparent earnings collapse is a tax charge, and the business underneath compounded.** Pre-tax income grew 22.5% in fiscal 2025 on 13.7% revenue growth. Anyone screening on reported earnings per share is looking at the wrong number.

🟢 **Guidance has been beaten in every quarter in the file, and the bad news was pre-announced.** The memory constraint was disclosed in February 2026, before it hit the numbers.

🟢 **Automotive is running ahead of its own target.** A record $1.33B quarter, up 38% year over year (reported 2026-04-29), passing a $5B annualised rate and guided to exit fiscal 2026 above a $6B rate, against an original $8B fiscal-2029 goal since raised to $10B. The fifth-generation chassis platform is described as the largest generation-to-generation content increase in company history, and the migration from selling chips to selling modules and software raises both revenue per car and margin.

🟢 **Pricing power is being exercised.** The 24 July 2026 report of double-digit price increases to customers is the direct answer to the cost-inflation question analysts kept asking, and it arrived within days of this review.

🟢 **The balance sheet and cash returns are conservative.** Net debt of $5.47B against $12.50B of annual free cash flow, a solvency score of 6.1, all free cash flow returned to shareholders, a quarterly dividend of $0.92 declared 17 July 2026, and a share count down about 7% in two years.

🟢 **Named counterparties, not just ambitions.** Meta and Microsoft as data-centre customers (2026-06-24), a long-term memory agreement with Micron for automotive (2026-07-16), a Volkswagen Group letter of intent spanning Audi and Porsche (2026-02-04), and BMW shipping the first full self-driving stack (2025-11-05).

## 7. Hidden signals

**The vocabulary migrated from "connectivity" to "compute."** In April 2025 the company described itself through modems and connectivity leadership. By April 2026 the self-description is "the world's best-performing central processing unit across smartphones, personal computers, automotive and soon the data centre," and the boast is a power range — "milliwatts to kilowatts." Qualcomm has stopped selling itself as a wireless company.

**A new voice at investor relations.** Mauricio Lopez-Hodoyan opened four consecutive calls; Brett Simpson, carrying a senior vice-president title, opens the 2026-04-29 call. A more senior investor-relations hire immediately before an investor day that resets long-term targets is a deliberate sequencing choice, not a coincidence.

**Capital allocation language loosened.** In April 2025, buybacks were raised to 100% of free cash flow because "given where the stock price is, it's an opportunity" — while "maintaining our strategic flexibility for M&A." That flexibility has since been spent: Alphawave ($2.4B), Arduino, Edge Impulse, Foundries.io, Ventana Micro Systems and Arcturus-class image-processing assets all closed inside the window. Asked on 2025-07-30 whether more would follow, the chief executive would only say "we're always going to be looking." A separately reported Tenstorrent approach was denied by that company's chief executive on 30 June 2026. The pattern is a company buying its way into the data centre at pace.

**The competitive answer changed shape.** In April 2025 the response to competitive questions was reassurance: share is stable, the landscape "has not changed for us at all." By April 2026 the framing is that the installed base of devices "were not built for" agent-style artificial intelligence — an argument that the whole market is about to be replaced, which is a far more aggressive posture than defending share.

**An unusually candid margin admission.** Asked on 2025-11-05 why chip-segment margins fell despite revenue growth, the chief financial officer did not reach for mix: "we are investing in the data center area… Data center is incremental to the investment profile that we have." That confirms the long-running promise to hold total operating expense flat has been broken deliberately — the new business is additive spending, and it will compress margins before it produces revenue.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a company defending a declining base, and it is not a clean compounder either. Handsets — roughly two-thirds of revenue — are flat to shrinking, structurally constrained by memory supply this year and by customer in-sourcing over the longer run. Against that, automotive is compounding at nearly 40%, internet-of-things is growing, and an entirely new data-centre business has been announced, staffed by acquisition, and guided to first revenue in the December 2026 quarter. The shape of the company in 2029 will be materially different from today's. That is the definition of a pivot, and pivots are where credibility gets tested rather than assumed.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Not the data-centre target, and not the memory shortage — both are already loudly debated. It is the licensing renewal. The licensing segment throws off roughly $4.0B of pre-tax profit at a 72% margin on $5.58B of revenue: about a third of company profit, from an asset with no factories and no cost of goods. Management has twice declined to say anything about the largest renewal beyond "we don't expect it to change." If that annuity resets down by a third, roughly $1.3B of pre-tax profit — more than the entire automotive segment earns today — disappears at the stroke of a pen, and no amount of data-centre optionality replaces it on the same timeline. Size the position for a licensing outcome you cannot currently observe.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and stable rather than widening.** The moat is genuinely two moats. The licensing business rests on an intangible-asset moat — a portfolio of patents essential to cellular standards — which is durable but capped: it cannot grow faster than global handset value, it has been flat at $5.3B–$6.4B of revenue for five years, and it is periodically renegotiated with counterparties who are individually large enough to fight. The chip business rests on a scale-and-engineering moat: a genuine performance lead in mobile processors and the associated neural-processing engines, reinforced by the cost of re-architecting an entire device platform. It is real — Samsung's baseline share moved *up* from 50% to 75% over years of competing with in-house silicon, and Xiaomi signed a multi-year premium agreement (2025-07-30) — but it is not wide, because the largest customer proved a determined buyer can leave, and the China market is explicitly shared with one strong competitor.

The evidence says stable, not eroding and not widening. Gross margin held at 55.4% and is described as stable; chip-segment pre-tax margin printed 29%; return on invested capital of 20–23% remains far above any plausible cost of capital; non-Apple chip revenue grew 18% in fiscal 2025. But return on invested capital has drifted down from its peak, research spending has risen to 21.4% of revenue, and management has confirmed the data-centre build is incremental expense. A franchise spending more to hold the same return is stable, not widening.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** Qualcomm is not on the losing side of the structural forces that impair terminal value in this book. Generative artificial intelligence does not displace it — the company's argument, and it is a credible one, is that running models on the device rather than in the cloud increases the silicon content of every phone, laptop, car and pair of glasses. The genuine structural risk is different and narrower: customer vertical integration. Apple's modem, Samsung's Exynos, and now ByteDance's reported in-house processor all describe the same pattern, in which Qualcomm's best customers become its competitors once volume justifies the design cost. That is a real, permanent tax on the growth rate, and it is why the licensing annuity — which taxes the industry regardless of whose chip is inside — matters so much to the terminal value. It is a headwind to be sized, not a melting base.

**So is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** A fear-print, with a caveat. The optical cheapness — a fair value of $59 and a margin of safety of -65% on the screener's earnings-based models — is a measurement error caused by a one-off tax charge, and the corrected picture is a business whose pre-tax profit compounded at about 30% a year for two years, trading at roughly 13 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation while its named peer group trades at 28 to 44 times. The caveat is that the discount is not the 65% the screen advertises; it is a more ordinary one, and it is being asked to survive two down quarters and one unobservable licensing negotiation.

Qualcomm is entering a market where Nvidia, Broadcom, Marvell and the cloud operators' own silicon teams are years ahead, and it is doing so with a chip that has not shipped.

Fifth, the arithmetic of the headline does not close. Management framed total revenue 'toward $100 billion' by fiscal 2029 against roughly $44B today and a three-year revenue growth rate of +0.1% a year. Their own component targets — about $40B non-handset, roughly $30B handset chips, about $6B licensing — sum to about $76B. The gap between the components and the headline is promotional.

Sixth, nobody inside is buying. Zero open-market purchases against 62 sales totalling 37,387 shares. After a 34% drawdown, from a management team that has just told the market its long-term outlook doubled, the absence of a single insider purchase is the loudest silence in the file.

Seventh, the setup is hostile. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index entered a bear market in mid-July, down more than 20% from its June record; Bank of America described long semiconductors on 15 July 2026 as the most crowded trade ever recorded in its survey; and 'artificial-intelligence bubble' became the number-one tail risk in the same survey for the first time. Qualcomm's earnings land on 29 July, the same day as the Federal Reserve decision and two of the largest cloud operators' capital-expenditure guides. If those guides disappoint, Qualcomm's entire re-rating thesis — the edge-and-data-centre artificial-intelligence story — de-rates with the group regardless of what Qualcomm itself reports.

What would confirm the bear: a July 29 guide for the September quarter below roughly $10B; any indication that the price increases are being met with share loss rather than acceptance; a licensing renewal disclosed at reduced scale; or a slip in the December-quarter data-centre shipment.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market comes down to one arithmetic error and one framing error.

The arithmetic error is the earnings base. Qualcomm screens as a company whose earnings per share fell 44% last year and has compounded downward at 23.9% a year for three years, which produces a fair value of $59 and a margin of safety of -65% across four separate valuation models. All four are fed the same corrupted input. Fiscal-2025 pre-tax income was $12.66B, up 22.5% on the prior year, and operating income rose 22.7%; what destroyed reported earnings per share was a one-off tax charge that lifted the effective rate to 56.2% after two years at roughly 2%. The trailing figure is already back to $9.32 and the latest quarter was up 173% year over year. Four models agreeing with one another is not corroboration when they share a single broken input. Anyone running a mechanical value screen on this name is measuring an accounting event.

The framing error is what the sell side is actually underwriting. The street consensus target is $216.25, the median $220, with 27 targets in the last quarter averaging $207.26 — but the newest marks are drifting down, not up: UBS cut to $190 on 20 July with the stock at $172.60, having been at $235 on 25 June. Consensus forward earnings growth is +1.2%. So the street is modelling a flat business at a modest premium — it is not, in any meaningful sense, underwriting the data-centre programme. That is the specific assumption we think is wrong in both directions. It is too pessimistic on the parts that already exist: automotive grew 38% year over year to a record $1.33B quarter, is passing a $5B annualised rate against an original $8B fiscal-2029 target, and is migrating from chips to modules-with-software at higher margin — that is not a flat business. And it is too complacent about the part that does not exist: more than $15B of fiscal-2029 data-centre revenue with no disclosed backlog is not something to model at zero *or* at face value, and the street has largely chosen zero.

The second disagreement is on the memory shortage. The street reads it as a demand problem. Management's own framing, repeated across two calls, is that it is a supply constraint layered on top of a favourable mix shift — when handset makers must ration scarce memory, they allocate it to premium and high-tier phones, which is precisely where Qualcomm's content per device is highest. The chief financial officer said it directly on 29 April 2026: if volume shifts up, 'that is usually a benefit for us.' A shortage that shrinks units while enriching mix is a very different thing from a demand recession, and the 24 July 2026 report that Qualcomm is pushing through double-digit price increases is evidence the company holds the pricing end of that relationship.

The third disagreement runs the other way, and it is why we are not more aggressive. The street is not pricing the licensing renewal at all, and neither is management discussing it. Roughly $4.0B of pre-tax profit — about a third of company profit at a 72% margin — sits inside a negotiation whose terms, timing and counterparty posture are entirely unobservable from outside. 'We don't expect it to change' (29 April 2026) is the strongest statement on the record. That is the one place where the market's complacency and ours coincide, and it is the risk that would break this thesis without warning.
forcing_function:
Three dated events, in order of proximity.

1. **29 July 2026, after the close — third-quarter fiscal 2026 results and September-quarter guidance.** Confirmed by the company's scheduling notice of 15 July. This is the near-term forcing function and it resolves three questions at once: whether the June quarter was the bottom in Chinese handset shipments as management claimed on 29 April; whether the double-digit price increases reported by Bloomberg on 24 July are being accepted by customers; and whether the December-quarter custom-silicon shipment to a large cloud operator is on schedule. Note the caution: it lands the same day as the Federal Reserve decision and the Microsoft and Meta capital-expenditure guides, so a company-specific good result can be drowned by a sector-wide bad one.

2. **The December 2026 quarter — first data-centre revenue.** Management stated on 29 April 2026 that it is 'entering the custom silicon space beginning our ramp with a leading hyperscaler' with 'initial shipments in the December quarter'. This is the event that converts the fiscal-2029 target from a slide into an income-statement line. Until a dollar of data-centre revenue is reported, the market is entitled to value that business at zero, and it broadly does. The first reported figure — whatever its size — is the moment the discount becomes indefensible or the bear case is proved.

3. **Undated but binding when it lands — the licensing renewal.** The largest licence in a segment producing about $4.0B of pre-tax profit is in renegotiation, confirmed as 'underway' on 4 February 2026 with no update since. This is the only event in the file that can move a third of company profit in a single disclosure, and it will arrive without a scheduled date. It is as likely to force a re-rating upward — by removing the overhang at unchanged scale — as downward.

On the activist and sum-of-the-parts lens: there is no realistic activist path here. The parts discount is real but is not the sort a shareholder campaign can unlock — nobody is going to argue that a company earning a 20-23% return on invested capital, returning 100% of free cash flow and retiring 7% of its shares in two years is misallocating capital. There is no governance reset available and no strategic process to force. The re-rating, if it comes, has to be earned through the income statement.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is unusually short and unusually dense, and it starts in two days.

The immediate hazard is the 29 July results themselves. Consensus is $2.22 of earnings per share on $9.68B of revenue — down about 20% and 7% year over year — so the quarter is guided to be bad and the question is only the September guide. Management called the June quarter the bottom for Chinese handset shipments on 29 April 2026; if that call is wrong, or if the memory constraint has worsened, the September guide comes in below roughly $10B and the shares have no valuation floor to fall back on. There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall here — net debt is $5.47B against $12.50B of annual free cash flow, and the solvency score of 6.1 is comfortably safe — so the risk is entirely to the multiple, not to the balance sheet.

The compounding hazard is the calendar around it. The print lands inside the densest event cluster of the year: the Federal Reserve meets 28-29 July under a chair whose December rate rise is still the priced base case, Microsoft and Meta report on 29 July and Apple and Amazon on 30 July, and those four capital-expenditure guides are the market's verdict on artificial-intelligence spending. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is already in a bear market, more than 20% below its June record; Bank of America's July survey called long semiconductors the most crowded trade ever recorded and put 'artificial-intelligence bubble' as the number-one tail risk for the first time. A hyperscaler guide-down on 29 or 30 July de-rates Qualcomm regardless of what Qualcomm itself reports, because the entire re-rating case is an artificial-intelligence-at-the-edge-and-in-the-data-centre story. Catalysts resolving inside this cluster tend to produce muted or delayed re-ratings; early-August landings are cleaner.

The slower hazards over the next three to nine months are three. First, the memory shortage is not forecast to resolve: memory makers have guided to satisfying only 50-70% of demand with shortages running into 2028, and management explicitly declined to predict when it ends ('we can't really predict if this will continue for 2027 or 2028', 4 February 2026). Fiscal 2027 could be a second constrained year. Second, the double-digit price increases reported on 24 July are a bet — if MediaTek does not follow, Qualcomm trades margin for share in the one market (China) where the competition is a genuine two-player fight. Third, the data-centre spend is incremental operating expense that lands before any revenue: the chief financial officer confirmed on 5 November 2025 that 'data center is incremental to the investment profile that we have', and research spending is already 21.4% of revenue. Margins compress first and recover only if the December-quarter shipment leads somewhere.

The unbounded hazard, with no date attached, is the licensing renewal. It could be disclosed at any time, in either direction, and roughly a third of company profit sits on the outcome.
positioning_washout:
Forced selling is not the mechanism here — there is no dividend cut, no index deletion and no covenant to breach — but the ownership base is unstable in a subtler and more relevant way, and part of the wash-out has already happened.

Qualcomm has just been through the mechanical part. The shares closed at $250 on 3 June 2026 and $165.94 on 27 July, a 34% fall in eight weeks on heavy volume — 47.1M shares on 18 June, 37.1M on 26 June, 34.9M on 25 June, against a recent daily norm nearer 10M. That is what a crowded trade unwinding looks like, and the timing is the tell: the largest volume days cluster around the 24 June Investor Day, which was good news. A stock that falls 19% in the month after doubling its long-term targets, on rising volume, is being sold by holders who do not care what the targets say. Bank of America's July survey describing long semiconductors as the most crowded trade ever recorded names the seller: momentum and thematic money that arrived for the artificial-intelligence trade and is leaving because the sector broke, not because Qualcomm did.

The remaining fragility is the composition of who is left. Qualcomm sits in a genuinely awkward place in the ownership landscape. Its 2.2% dividend yield (a $0.92 quarterly payment declared 17 July 2026, payable 24 September) and 7.2% free-cash-flow yield make it a natural holding for income and quality-value funds — but those investors do not want a company spending 21.4% of revenue on research to enter the data-centre market against Nvidia. Meanwhile growth and artificial-intelligence funds will not own it at a 15-times multiple with two-thirds of revenue in handsets and a fiscal-2026 earnings decline. Each cohort has a reason to sell into the other's thesis. The recent thirteen-F filings visible in the tape are one-directional: Allspring cut 38.7%, Bank of Nova Scotia 20.3%, Bradley Foster 12.4%.

The insider record confirms nobody internal is stepping in: zero open-market purchases against 62 sales totalling 37,387 shares. The buyer of last resort is the company itself — Qualcomm returns 100% of free cash flow to shareholders and has retired about 7% of the share count in two years, which puts a persistent bid of roughly $2B a quarter underneath the stock. That is real support, but it is a slow bid, not a floor.

The practical implication: a disappointing 29 July guide would land on a shareholder base with no natural holder of the story, and the second leg down could be sharper than the first. Conversely, if the guide is merely adequate, the marginal seller has already left.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good business that has just been sold hard for reasons that have very little to do with it, priced at a real but ordinary discount, two days ahead of a print it has already warned will be weak. All three of those clauses matter, and they pull in different directions.

Start with what is genuinely mispriced. The screened case for Qualcomm — a fair value of $59, a margin of safety of -65%, earnings falling 44% — is an artefact. Fiscal-2025 pre-tax income was $12.66B, up 22.5%, and the reported earnings collapse was a single tax charge that pushed the effective rate to 56.2% after two years near 2%. Four of the five valuation models the screener runs are fed that broken number and therefore agree with one another for the same wrong reason. The corrected business earns a 20-23% return on invested capital and a 55.4% gross margin, generates $12.50B of free cash flow against a $175B market value, carries only $5.47B of net debt, and returns every dollar of that cash to shareholders. It trades at 13 times enterprise value to EBITDA while Texas Instruments trades at 28.7, Marvell at 35.4, MediaTek at 42.2 and Broadcom at 43.9. The peer file's premise that MediaTek is the cheap comparable is simply out of date.

Now the discipline. Part of that peer gap is earned, not stolen: those companies already report artificial-intelligence data-centre revenue and Qualcomm reports none. The fiscal-2029 target of more than $15B was announced a month ago with named customers but no backlog, and first shipments are a December-quarter event. Valuing that programme somewhere between the market's zero and management's face value is the whole of the analytical work, and doing it honestly produces a base-case sum-of-the-parts of about $202 — roughly 22% above today's $166, below the street's $216 consensus, and below the screener's own cash-flow fair value of $206. That is a real discount. It is not a fat one, and it is not the 65% the screen advertises.

Against that sits an adverse case at $130 that is about equally far away. Getting there requires the memory constraint to persist through fiscal 2027, the licensing annuity to reset lower, and the data-centre programme to be worth nothing — three things that could each happen and would compound if they did. The upside tail at $276 is fatter than the downside tail, so the distribution is right-skewed, but the base case is close to symmetric and there is no structural floor: Qualcomm carries net debt, not net cash, so nothing in the balance sheet stops the price.

On timing, the regime is the deciding vote. Earnings land 29 July, inside the densest event cluster of the year — the Federal Reserve on 28-29 July, Microsoft and Meta on 29 July, Apple and Amazon on 30 July — with the semiconductor index already in a bear market, the sector named as the most crowded trade ever recorded, and artificial-intelligence capital expenditure sitting as the market's number-one tail risk. Both legs of this thesis resolve on that single shared factor: the data-centre leg obviously, and the handset leg through memory pricing, which is itself a derivative of artificial-intelligence data-centre demand. A book that requires its positions to resolve on independent drivers cannot treat this as an independent one. Buying two days before a guided-down print, inside that cluster, is paying for optionality on someone else's earnings call.

So: wait for the wash-out, and name it. Two specific developments would change the call. The first is the 29 July guide itself — a September-quarter revenue guide at or above roughly $10.5B, together with confirmation that the price increases are holding and the December-quarter data-centre shipment is on schedule, removes the near-term uncertainty and makes the discount actionable at whatever price follows. The second is price: a guide-down that takes the shares toward $140-145 would put the stock at roughly 13 times a trough earnings figure with the data-centre business free, which is a materially better entry than today's.

Separately, and this is the more important number for a value book: judged purely on the price against the parts and on the quality of the numbers underneath, ignoring the calendar entirely, this scores well. The forensics are clean — seven guidance beats in seven quarters, headwinds pre-announced with figures attached rather than explained afterwards, a balance sheet with five months of free cash flow in net debt, and an apparent earnings collapse that dissolves on inspection. The moat is narrow rather than wide: a patent annuity that cannot grow faster than the handset market and gets renegotiated, plus a genuine engineering lead in a market shared with one strong competitor and populated by customers who periodically become competitors. It is stable rather than eroding — margins are holding, non-Apple chip revenue grew 18% last year, automotive is compounding at 38% — but the company is spending more (21.4% of revenue on research) to hold the same return, which is the definition of stable rather than widening. What withholds the top mark is not the business and not the numbers; it is that a 22% discount to a carefully-built parts value is a good price, not a great one. If this traded at $140 the answer would be different.

interrogator_dossier:
# QUALCOMM Incorporated (QCOM) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Listing analysed:** NASDAQ ordinary shares (QCOM), quoted in US dollars · **Reporting currency:** US dollars
**Live price used:** $165.99 (NASDAQ, 2026-07-27; previous close $166.97; 52-week range $121.99–$259.92; market value about $175B)
**Transcripts reviewed:** five consecutive quarterly earnings calls — 2025-04-30 (fiscal Q2 2025), 2025-07-30 (fiscal Q3 2025), 2025-11-05 (fiscal Q4 and full-year 2025), 2026-02-04 (fiscal Q1 2026), 2026-04-29 (fiscal Q2 2026)

A word on what has just happened to the price, because it frames everything below. Qualcomm closed at $250 on 3 June 2026 and trades at $166 today — a fall of about 34% in eight weeks. Nothing the company said caused it. In the middle of that decline, on 24 June, management held an Investor Day and roughly doubled its most important long-term target. The stock jumped 8% the next day, to $205, and then kept bleeding. The drawdown is a sector event — the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index entered a bear market in mid-July, down more than 20% from its June record — landing on a company whose own numbers are about to get worse for two quarters for reasons management flagged in advance. The committee's job is to separate those two things.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across these five calls the story does not wander; it widens, in three deliberate steps, and then runs into a supply shock the company does not control.

**Spring 2025 — diversification as defence.** The 2025-04-30 call is a company managing a known subtraction. Apple is designing Qualcomm's modem out of its phones, and the entire narrative is built to answer "what replaces it." The frame is a set of fiscal-2029 targets set at a 2024 investor day: $22B of combined automotive and internet-of-things revenue, $8B of that automotive, $4B from personal computers, $2B from extended reality (headsets and smart glasses). The chief executive's closing line is defensive in the most literal sense — "we always ask ourselves, is our technology relevant?" The chief financial officer explains that operating expense is being *moved*, not added: investment shifts out of handsets into the new areas while total spending holds flat. That is a disciplined, low-risk pivot, and it is what the company was selling in April 2025.

**Summer to autumn 2025 — the data centre arrives.** The 2025-07-30 call introduces an entirely new leg: Qualcomm is building artificial-intelligence inference accelerator cards and custom server processors, has agreed to buy Alphawave (a high-speed connectivity intellectual-property business) for $2.4B, and is "in advanced discussions with a leading hyperscaler" — one of the giant cloud operators. Revenue, management says, would begin in fiscal 2028. By the 2025-11-05 call the products have names (the AI200 and AI250 chips), a first customer (HUMAIN, the Saudi venture, targeting 200 megawatts of deployment from 2026), and a promise of a dedicated investor event. Asked directly whether this is bigger than the $2B extended-reality target, the chief executive answers plainly: "it's upside on that number… a potential multibillion-dollar revenue opportunity in a couple of years."

**Winter 2026 — the memory shock.** The 2026-02-04 call opens with record revenue of $12.3B and then immediately introduces the constraint that now dominates: memory chip makers are diverting capacity to high-bandwidth memory for artificial-intelligence data centres, creating an industry-wide shortage that will "define the overall scale of the handset industry through the fiscal year." Chinese handset makers respond by drawing down chip inventory. This is the single most important disclosure in the five calls, and management made it *before* the numbers deteriorated, not after.

**Spring 2026 — the pivot becomes the story.** By 2026-04-29 the language has changed shape. The chief executive opens not with results but with a thesis: "we are in a period of profound change, and it may not yet seem obvious to the financial community." Agent-style artificial intelligence — software that runs continuously in the background and carries out multi-step tasks — is presented as a device-replacement cycle across phones, personal computers, cars and robots. Robotics is formally announced as a business. Custom silicon for a leading cloud operator is confirmed with first shipments guided for the December 2026 quarter. Sixth-generation wireless is introduced as a 2028-2030 driver. And the handset business is described honestly as under-shipping real demand, with the China trough called for the June quarter.

**What was quietly dropped.** Two things. The personal-computer target of $4B by fiscal 2029 has gone almost silent; the market-share figure — about 9% of Windows laptops above $600 in the United States and the top five European markets — was repeated verbatim in two consecutive quarters (April and July 2025) and then stopped being quoted. Repeating a number and then dropping it is usually a sign it stopped improving. Second, the extended-reality target has been overtaken by events in the other direction: smart glasses are now discussed as an inflection, with design counts running from 15 (April 2025) to 19 (July 2025) to 30 (November 2025) to more than 40 personal-artificial-intelligence devices (February 2026).

**Where it landed.** At the 24 June 2026 Investor Day the fiscal-2029 non-handset revenue target went from $22B to about $40B: data centre above $15B, automotive raised roughly 25% to $10B, with adjusted earnings per share above $18 and total revenue framed toward $100B. Meta and Microsoft were named as data-centre customers. This is a genuinely different company from the one described in April 2025.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

This is where the screener's own inputs need repairing before anything else can be judged.

**The headline earnings collapse is a tax artefact, not an operating one.** The screener shows fiscal-2025 earnings per share of $5.01, down 44.2% year over year, and a three-year compound decline of 23.9%. That looks like a business falling apart. It is not what happened. Pulling the audited income statements:

| Fiscal year | Revenue | Pre-tax income | Tax expense | Effective tax rate | Net income | Diluted EPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | $35.82B | $7.44B | $0.10B | 1.4% | $7.23B | $6.42 |
| 2024 | $38.96B | $10.34B | $0.23B | 2.2% | $10.14B | $8.98 |
| 2025 | $44.28B | $12.66B | $7.12B | 56.2% | $5.54B | $5.01 |

Pre-tax income — the number that measures the actual business — grew 39% in fiscal 2024 and a further 22.5% in fiscal 2025, compounding at about 30% a year over two years. Operating income rose from $10.07B to $12.36B in fiscal 2025, up 22.7%. What destroyed reported earnings per share was a one-off tax charge that pushed the effective rate to 56% after two years at roughly 2%. The trailing-twelve-month figure has already recovered to $9.32 as that charge rolls out of the window, and the latest quarter's earnings per share was up 173% year over year — which is the same artefact running in reverse.

This matters because it contaminates four of the five valuation models the screener runs. The earnings-power, Graham and fifteen-percent-return models all show a margin of safety of -100%, and the Buffett model returns a fair value of $59 against a $166 price. Those models are being fed a tax-crushed earnings figure. The one model built on cash flow rather than reported earnings — the discounted cash-flow model, at $206 — is the only one whose input was not broken. When four models built on the same corrupted input agree with each other, that is not confirmation; it is one error counted four times.

**Growth claims versus delivery.**

| Management claim (call, date) | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Second consecutive year of greater than 15% growth in total non-Apple chip revenue" (2025-07-30) | Fiscal 2025 delivered 18%, above the claim; chip-segment revenue $38.37B, up 16% | Under-promised, over-delivered |
| Automotive on track for $8B by fiscal 2029 (throughout) | Automotive grew 36% in fiscal 2025; passed a $5B annualised rate in the March 2026 quarter; record $1.33B quarter, up 38% year over year | Ahead of schedule — target since raised to $10B |
| "Close to 30% margin this year… no change to our long-term target" (2025-07-30) | Chip-segment pre-tax margin printed 29% in the September 2025 quarter, at the high end of guidance; group gross margin 55.4% and described as stable | Delivered |
| 100% of free cash flow returned to shareholders (2025-04-30) | Trailing free cash flow $12.50B against a $175B market value — a 7.2% free-cash-flow yield; diluted share count down from 1.130B (fiscal 2024) to about 1.053B today | Delivered; roughly 7% of the company retired in two years |
| Personal computers: "$4B by fiscal 2029", 150 designs (2025-11-05) | No revenue disclosure for the personal-computer line; the one hard market-share datapoint (about 9%) was repeated then dropped | Unverifiable — the weakest claim in the file |
| Data centre "$15B+ by fiscal 2029" (Investor Day, 2026-06-24) | Zero revenue today; first custom-silicon shipments guided for the December 2026 quarter; no binding backlog disclosed | Entirely forward — see red flags |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify.** The $100B revenue framing. Trailing revenue is about $44B. Reaching $100B by fiscal 2029 requires the whole non-handset build-out to land *and* the handset base to hold, in a business whose three-year revenue growth rate is +0.1% a year. Management's own arithmetic is more modest than the headline: $40B non-handset plus a roughly $30B handset chip business plus $6B of licensing gets to about $76B, not $100B.

**Where the numbers are richer than the story.** Returns and balance sheet. Return on equity of 52.2% and return on invested capital of 23% (the screener's figures; the trailing-twelve-month calculation puts return on invested capital at 20.1%) are earned on a balance sheet carrying only $5.47B of net debt against $12.50B of annual free cash flow — about five months of cash generation. Solvency scores 6.1 on the Altman scale, comfortably safe. Research and development runs at 21.4% of revenue, which is where the future is being bought.

**The near-term reality check.** Consensus for the July 29 quarter is $2.22 of earnings per share on $9.68B of revenue — down about 20% and 7% respectively against the same quarter last year. Fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings per share look set to land near $11 against fiscal 2025's roughly $12. This is a down year, and management told us why in February.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Rising on strategy, falling on the near-term — and the two have decoupled.**

- **2025-04-30 — guarded.** "As we navigate those times, this is a company that is not — it's experienced a little of uncertainty. We always ask ourselves, is our technology relevant?" That is a chief executive answering a question nobody asked out loud. Language is defensive: navigate, uncertainty, relevant.
- **2025-07-30 — opening a door.** The data-centre section is hedged with care: "while we are in the early stages of this expansion," "if successful, we expect revenues to begin in the fiscal '28 time frame." Conditional verbs throughout.
- **2025-11-05 — assertive.** "We're probably one of the few companies among all the semiconductor companies that can go from 5 watts to 500 watts." Products have part numbers, a customer has a megawatt figure, and an investor event is promised. The conditionals are gone.
- **2026-02-04 — split.** Record revenue delivered with confidence; the memory constraint delivered without spin. On whether the shortage runs into 2027 or 2028: "We can't really predict." That is an honest non-answer, and it is worth more than a confident guess.
- **2026-04-29 — highest conviction of the five calls, on the long term only.** "We are in a period of profound change, and it may not yet seem obvious to the financial community" is a chief executive telling the market it is wrong. Simultaneously the handset commentary is the most cautious in the set: under-shipping demand, calling a bottom, sell-side models for the Apple chip business validated at "a little over $2 billion" for fiscal 2027.

The shift from offensive to defensive language happened in one place only — handsets — while the language around everything else moved decisively the other way. That is the signature of a real pivot rather than a cover story.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The Apple licence renewal — deflected twice, and it is the single largest unquantified item.** On 2026-02-04, asked directly, the answer was: "whenever we see a renewal date on the horizon, we start discussions very well in advance. The licensing segment produced $5.58B of revenue at a 72% pre-tax margin in fiscal 2025 — roughly $4.0B of pre-tax profit, about a third of the company's total — and its largest single contributor is up for renegotiation with a counterparty that has spent five years reducing its dependence on Qualcomm.

**Margin under memory inflation — asked repeatedly, answered obliquely.** Analysts pressed on this three times (2025-11-05, 2026-02-04, 2026-04-29). The answers all route to the same place: premium mix is a margin benefit, so a smaller but richer market is fine. That is true as far as it goes, and the price action outside the calls now supports it — Bloomberg reported on 24 July 2026 that Qualcomm has told customers it will raise prices by a double-digit percentage. But the calls never quantified the cost headwind.
